As-built porosity defects were characterized for Parameter sets A and C using X-ray computed
tomography (XCT) with 140 kV and 80 µA on a North Star Imaging X50 machine here with 6.60
µm/pixel ± 0.33 µm/pixel spatial resolution. All XCT data was post-processed using eFX1 Software

characterization was completed only for parameter sets A and C where defect density was
expected to be the lowest and highest, respectively. Data visualization was completed using
ParaView [44].

The shape of the external surfaces, as well as the internal pores, along the gauge sections of the
Specimens A and C were characterized using X-ray computed tomography (XCT). The XCT
measurements were performed using a North Star Imaging X50 machine. A resolution of 6.60
µm/pixel ± 0.33 µm/pixel was chosen, and the entire gauge section was imaged within a single
field-of-view (FOV). Specimens A and C were measured simultaneously (in the same FOV) to
reduce the acquisition time of the X-ray radiographs. X-ray transparent material (i.e., folded
paper) was sandwiched between the specimens to ensure that the individual specimens could be
easily  separated  and  identified  during  post-processing  of  the  reconstructed  images.
Reconstruction of the radiographs was also completed using North Star Imaging (proprietary)
software: efX Software Suite Version 2.3.4. Additional settings used during the acquisition of the
XCT radiographs can be found in Table A1.

The reconstructed images were further post-processed using IMPPY3D [45], which is an open-
source Python library developed at NIST. First, the ring artifacts were removed from the grayscale
images, followed by non-local means denoising [46]. Then, the images were segmented using a
global threshold value, resulting in a binarized image stack where white pixels correspond to
solid, metallic material. A before-and-after example of segmenting a reconstructed image is
illustrated in Figure 15 .

After segmentation, the image stack was converted into a three-dimensional (3D) voxel model.
Each voxel represents an extruded pixel implying an equal width, height, and length of 6.60 µm.
Fully enclosed pores were identified by inverting the values of the segmented image stack. Due
to the memory demand required to store so many voxels, the 3D models of Specimens A and C
were transformed into surface meshes using the marching cubes algorithm [47]. Individual pores
were left as voxels however. Quantitative metrics were also calculated from the segmented
images, such as equivalent spherical volumes of the pores and the overall porosity of the
specimens.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,

search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.

Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Abstract:
Recent developments in metallic additive manufacturing (AM) processes for the production of high-performance industrial pieces have been hampered by the limited availability of reliably processable or printable alloys. To date, most of the alloys used in AM are commercial grades that have been previously optimized for different manufacturing techniques. This study aims to design new alloys specifically tailored for AM processes, to minimize defects in the final products and to optimize their properties. A computational approach is proposed to design novel and optimized austenitic alloy compositions. This method integrates a suite of predictive tools, including machine learning, calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) and physical models, all piloted by a multi-objective genetic algorithm. Within this framework, several material-dependent criteria are examined and their impact on properties and on the occurrence of defects is identified. To validate our approach, experimental tests are performed on a selected alloy composition: powder is produced by gas atomization and samples are fabricated by laser powder bed fusion. The microstructure and mechanical properties of the alloys are evaluated and its printability is compared with a commercial 316L stainless steel taken as a reference. The optimized alloy performs similarly to 316L in terms of coefficient of thermal expansion, hardness and elongation, but has a 17% lower yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (UTS), indicating that further optimization is required.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Supply chain challenges and health concerns have spurred the
                development of new Co-free, Cr-containing maraging steels with several new alloys
                already commercialized. These alloys are a less expensive and more sustainable form
                of the currently used Co-containing maraging steels C300 and C350. However, Co-free,
                Cr-containing maraging steels exhibit reduced strengths after heat treatment
                compared to current Co-containing alloys. New processing pathways are required to
                create microstructures able to reach parity with existing Co-containing or
                Ti-strengthened maraging steels and enable their replacement with sustainable
                alternatives. This work looks at using changes to laser beam powder bed fusion
                (PBF-LB) build parameters of the Co-free, Cr-containing maraging steel M789 to alter
                the as-built microstructure and provide new avenues for reaching parity with
                existing Co-containing maraging steels. Modelling of the PBF-LB build process
                suggests considerable changes in thermal history, and thereby likely unique
                evolution in solidification and solid state microstructures. Characterization of
                as-built material however showed little-to-no impact of build parameters on the
                solid state or solidification microstructures, suggesting M789 and other alloys
                experience phase transformations that are resilient to build parameter selection.
                Differences in porosity content between parameter sets obscured any changes in
                material properties during uniaxial tension and hardness testing. Despite these
                defects, multiple parameter sets produced material with as-built tensile strengths
                comparable to C300 maraging steels, demonstrating M789 can be a feasible alternative
                of C300 in as-built material applications. Future considerations on using heat
                treatments and implementing HIP to remove porosity defects are discussed as avenues
                to identify processing routes which boost the mechanical properties of M789 and
                other Co-free, Cr-containing alloys. Future work on better understanding the solid
                state transformations of M789 are also discussed, especially with implications on
                the resilience of this alloy to changes in build parameters and the development of
                other AM-resilient alloys.</jats:p>

cycle starts with the
deposition of a thin powder layer, achieved through the coordinated movement of the
powder dispenser, the downward displacement of the build platform, and the action of
the recoater blade, which spreads a uniform layer of metal powder across the build
area. The vertical displacement of the build platform, typically between 20 and 100
µm per layer, determines the layer thickness. Following deposition, a laser beam
selectively melts and fuses regions of the powder bed according to the predeﬁned scan
pattern generated during slicing. This sequence of powder deposition and selective
melting is repeated layer by layer until the component is completed (Figure 1). The
process  is conducted in a controlled inert atmosphere, typically maintained by a
continuous ﬂow of argon gas to prevent oxidation and contamination.



                                     3Figure 1: Schematic outlining the PBF-LB process. The arrows indicate the movement
of the diﬀerent platforms and the recoater during the build cycle.

2.2 Eﬀect of Processing Parameters

There are many process parameters that control the PBF-LB process, but the most
signiﬁcant ones that deﬁne part consolidation are the laser power (P), laser scan speed
(ν), hatch spacing (h), and powder layer thickness (t). These parameters are typically
formulated into an empirical relation, which provides an estimation of the energy input
into the material. This is termed as VED (volumetric energy density). The expression
is as follows:

                              ௉
                        VED =                                               (1)
                                             ఔ.௛.௧

where P is the laser power (W), ν is the scan speed (mm/s), h is the hatch spacing,
and  t  is the powder layer thickness, as illustrated in Figure 2. From a processing
standpoint, this metric only provides a basic understanding about the parameter set
in terms of achievable densiﬁcation in the part, as it does not consider other parameters
such as the  laser intensity  distribution, spot  size or material speciﬁc constants.
Improved models explaining the heat ﬂow during PBF-LB processing have been
proposed including the above-mentioned parameters [22], but further research needs to
be conducted in this regard.





                                     4Figure 2: Schematic outlining the main process parameters in PBF-LB.

Another parameter that aﬀects part consolidation is the employed scan strategy, which
deﬁnes the path and orientation of the laser scan vectors during printing. Many studies
have observed pronounced eﬀects in the microstructure, residual stresses, and defect
formation in various PBF-LB processed alloys with the modiﬁcation of scan strategies
[23,24]. Typically, a single exposed slice has two main components, in terms of scanning
and exposure, namely the core and contour, where the former refers to a scanning of
the entire slice, with the latter being the exposure of the outline of the part. For the
core exposure part, a scan rotation is applied between successive layers, where typically
a 67° rotation angle is chosen, as it results in the highest number of orientations before
the original orientation is repeated. This strategy has shown to result in lower residual
stress and break down the columnar microstructure [25]. In addition to scan rotation,
some strategies also include dividing the scan area into equal sections. This is typically
achieved by employing a stripe or island strategy and are used to ensure a uniform
scan vector length across the scanned region [26].

2.3 Thermal Phenomena in PBF-LB

During the PBF-LB process, there are diﬀerent thermal phenomena that occur, that
aﬀect the processing, and the local thermal history experienced during the process.
These are typically classiﬁed in two stages: i) melting and solidiﬁcation of the powder,
and ii) intrinsic tempering due to cyclic heating from the subsequently deposited layers.


                                     5In PBF-LB, during a laser-matter interaction event, the laser irradiates particles on
the powder bed, turning them into a molten pool of liquid. This pool is carried at the
tip of the laser scan path, melting the preceding powder. During this process, heat is
transferred both into the surrounding powder particles and the underlying bulk,
resulting in a fusion zone and a heat aﬀected zone, see Figure 3. After the laser beam
has passed, the melt pool solidiﬁes. This series of events occur within a timeframe
ranging from micro-seconds to milli-seconds (10 -6 – 10 -3 s), depending on the laser
exposure time, leading to extremely high heating and cooling rates [27].

The proﬁle of the melt pool and the mode of heat transfer during PBF-LB are governed
by  the  applied  laser parameters and  are  generally  classiﬁed  into two  regimes:
conduction mode and keyhole mode melting. In the conduction mode, shallow melt
pools are formed, with heat primarily conducted into the surrounding material [28]. In
contrast,  keyhole mode  melting  produces  deeper  melt  pools  due  to  localized
vaporization and recoil pressure, that can lead to spherical pores near the base of the
melt pool [29]. By carefully adjusting the laser parameters, the melting mode can be
controlled to achieve optimal densiﬁcation. However, improper parameter selection may
lead to process instabilities and the formation of porosity-related defects within the
material. These defects and their eﬀects on the material will be detailed in Section 2.4.





Figure 3: Schematic illustrating the local thermal history, highlighting the diﬀerent
zones that occur during layer melting and where untempered and tempered martensite
is found in low alloy steel specimens.

The thermal history  in the PBF-LB process  is primarily governed by the heat
transferred to the underlying material. In regions adjacent to the melt pool, the
material experiences temperatures exceeding the Ac3 temperature  (for  low-alloy
steels), and in some cases, approaching the melting point. This region undergoes re-
austenitization followed by rapid quenching, forming the re-austenitized zone (as


                                     6illustrated in Figure 3). Beneath this, the material is heated to temperatures below
Ac3 and experiences rapid tempering each time a new layer is deposited. This repeated
heating and cooling produces a cyclic thermal eﬀect, with the peak temperature
progressively decaying with increasing distance from the heat source (i.e., the newly
formed melt pool). Additionally, a macro-scale tempering eﬀect  arises from the
accumulation of heat within the solidiﬁed material. This phenomenon typically extends
over a depth of approximately 10–20 layers, where the temperature may approach that
of the build platform [30].

2.4 Defects in PBF-LB

As discussed previously, the choice of process parameters can inﬂuence the formation
of defects during the PBF-LB process. These are typically classiﬁed into three types i)
lack of fusion porosity, ii) keyhole porosity, and iii) gas porosity. Lack of fusion porosity
is caused by either an insuﬃcient overlap between deposited layers (inter-layer lack of
fusion), or between two tracks in the same layer (inter – hatch lack of fusion). This can
be mitigated by either tuning the laser power or scan speed to create large enough
melt pools to create suﬃcient overlap, or by reducing the hatch distance between two
tracks.





Figure 4: Defects in the PBF-LB process: a) lack of fusion porosity, b) gas porosity,
and c) keyhole porosity as observed during X-ray imaging.



                                     7Lack of fusion porosity it typically composed of oblong – shaped pores with sharp
corners that can act as stress concentrations when subjected to loading [31]. Keyhole
porosity is a result of a collapse of a vapor depression during keyhole melting [29].
These pores are typically spherical and are less detrimental to the mechanical response
than lack of fusion porosity. Keyhole porosity is generally mitigated by reducing the
energy input, for example by lowering the laser power, increasing the scan speed, or
enlarging the beam diameter. Gas porosity consists of small, rounded pores that
primarily originate from entrapped gas within the powder feedstock or previously
formed lack of fusion pores. The gas trapped within these pores is released during
remelting by the subsequent laser scan but becomes re-entrapped within the molten
pool [32]. These pores are spherical in shape and are smaller than keyhole pores, and
they are distributed randomly throughout the deposited material [33].

the PBF-LB process, as it is one of the major drivers for structural applications within
more  cost-sensitive  industries  like  automotive,  railway  and  consumer  goods
manufacturing. Strategies to achieve this have included the use

Apart from densiﬁcation, there has been a major drive to increase the productivity of
the PBF-LB process, as it is one of the major drivers for structural applications within
more  cost-sensitive  industries  like  automotive,  railway  and  consumer  goods

systems [34], higher power lasers [35], with one popular approach being parameter
optimization, especially by increasing the layer thickness. This approach has proven
feasible in several well-established PBF-LB alloy systems. However, this typically
comes with a drawback of lower resolution and increased surface roughness and is
typically accompanied by a slight drop in mechanical performance [36–39].





                                     83 Low-Alloy Steels and Tool Steels

Low alloy steels are a class of iron-based alloys which have a total alloying content of
< 10 wt.%, and are typically alloyed with elements such as Cr, Mn, Si, Mo, Ni, V, Nb,
etc. They are also classiﬁed by their carbon content as either low carbon (up to 0.3 wt.
% C) or medium carbon (0.3 – 0.6 wt. % C) grades. In comparison to plain carbon
steels, these materials exhibit better mechanical properties due to their alloying
additions which improve hardenability, precipitation and solid solution strengthening.
These additions also aﬀect the phase stability of the Fe – matrix, with elements like C,
N, Ni, Mn and Co stabilizing the austenite phase, and elements like Cr, Si, Mo, etc.
stabilizing the ferrite phase [40].

On the other hand, tool steels are a specialized class of high-carbon and alloy steels
designed speciﬁcally for making tools, dies, and molds. Their deﬁning characteristics
include high hardness and wear resistance, good toughness, and heat resistance [41].
These properties are achieved by adding speciﬁc alloying elements like W, Mo, V, and
Cr, which form hard carbide particles within the steel matrix [42]. Tool steels are
classiﬁed into several groups based on their composition or application, such as cold-
work (like A-series or D-series), hot-work (H-series), and high-speed steels (T-series or
M-series), each optimized for speciﬁc manufacturing tasks  like cutting, stamping,
forging, or molding [41].

Due to these alloying additions, the range of properties achievable by these steels is
quite broad, but another aspect to consider  is the processing route. Traditional
processing methods involve subjecting the material to high temperature (above Ac3)
and then controlling the transformation product by adjusting the cooling rate. If the
material is cooled slowly, it results in a mixture of ferrite (alpha – Fe) and cementite
(Fe3C) in the ﬁnal microstructure. But with an increase in cooling rates, it transforms
to bainite at intermediate cooling rates, and martensite at high cooling rates. These
diﬀerent microstructures provide their unique beneﬁts to the mechanical response and
are chosen based on the intended application [43].

This study focuses on two such materials, namely SSAB AM Engineering, a low-alloyed
steel composition from SSAB, and Osprey® HWTS50, a lean hot work tool steel
designed by Sandvik Osprey.

3.1 Martensite

Martensite is a supersaturated, metastable phase that forms in steels when austenite
is rapidly cooled, or quenched, at rates suﬃcient to suppress diﬀusional transformations
such as ferrite or pearlite formation. It is characterized by a body-centered tetragonal

                                     9(BCT)  crystal  structure,  resulting  from  the  shear-dominant,  lattice-distortive,
diﬀusionless transformation of face-centered cubic (FCC) austenite [44]. In low-alloy
and tool steels, the morphology of martensite (typically lath-like or plate-like) depends
on the carbon content, with lower carbon levels promoting the formation of lath
martensite.

The microstructure of lath martensite typically consists of laths organized into blocks
and packets within  prior austenite  grains, with each packet sharing a common
crystallographic orientation relationship with the parent austenite, often described by
the Kurdjumov–Sachs relationship ({111}γ-Fe | | {101}α’-Fe) [45]. The size of individual
martensite laths is considered to be independent of both carbon content and cooling
rate [46]. In contrast, the dimensions of blocks and packets are strongly inﬂuenced by
these parameters, with ﬁner morphologies typically observed at higher carbon contents
and faster cooling rates [47]. The prior austenite grain size also plays a crucial role in
determining  the  resulting  martensitic  substructure, with  larger  austenite  grains
allowing the formation of coarser blocks and packets. Conversely, ﬁner austenite grains
increase the number of potential nucleation sites and restrict the growth of individual
martensitic variants, leading to a more reﬁned and homogeneous hierarchical structure
[48].





Figure 5: Schematic illustrating the hierarchical structure of martensite. The calculation
was performed using MTEX ORTools in MATLAB® [49].

3.2 Tempering of Martensite

The high dislocation density and carbon trapped in solid solution give martensite its
exceptional hardness and strength but also make it inherently brittle [50]. Heating
during tempering allows carbon diﬀusion and carbide precipitation, relieving stresses
and reducing brittleness, thereby improving toughness and ductility while retaining
high strength for structural applications. Tempering of martensitic steels involves
heating  below  the  austenite  phase  transition  (Ac1).  During  tempering,  the

                                     10microstructure evolves from a supersaturated and highly strained martensitic phase to
a stabilized ferritic matrix containing ﬁnely dispersed carbides, with alloying elements
inﬂuencing both the transformation kinetics and the types of carbides that form [51].

In the context of tool steels (Paper II), tempering is a critical heat treatment step that
tailors the balance between hardness, toughness, and dimensional stability required for
                                     11demanding applications such as cutting, forming, and die operations  [10,58]. At
elevated tempering temperatures, substitutional alloying elements partition to carbon-
rich regions and form thermodynamically stable secondary  carbides. The speciﬁc
carbide type depends on the alloying element’s atomic size, chemical aﬃnity for carbon,
and diﬀusivity [56]. Strong carbide formers such as Cr, Mo, W, V, and Nb promote
M2C, M6C, M7C3, M23C6, and MC types, providing ﬁne dispersions responsible for
secondary hardening and enhanced high-temperature strength  [59]. However, the
tempering response of PBF-LB processed low-alloy steels requires further investigation,
as it is strongly inﬂuenced by both the initial microstructural condition and the speciﬁc
parameters of the tempering treatment.

3.3 PBF-LB Microstructure

Due to the high cooling rates coupled with the previously discussed thermal cycling
observed in PBF-LB, low alloy steels exhibit a tempered martensitic microstructure in
the  as-built  state  [12],  with some  studies showing  the  presence  of a  bainitic
microstructure [7]. The observed microstructure diﬀers from that of conventionally
processed quenched and tempered martensite, exhibiting distinct structural features
across multiple length scales.





Figure 6: PBF-LB processed low alloy steel microstructure at diﬀerent length scales. a)
Example of overlapping melt pool boundaries showing the diﬀerent heat aﬀected zones,
b) EBSD phase map showing martensitic  blocks, c) SEM-STEM image showing
martensitic laths and ﬁne nano-sized carbides.

At  low  magniﬁcation,  the  microstructure  exhibits  the  characteristic  melt  pool
morphology of PBF-LB processed materials, featuring overlapping melt pools and
distinct dark bands along their boundaries, which are preferentially attacked during
etching [8]. These boundary regions correspond to re-austenitized, or severely tempered
zones formed due  to  their  close  proximity  to  the melt  pool. At  intermediate
magniﬁcation, the microstructure reveals a ﬁne block-like morphology without any
pronounced crystallographic texture relative to the build direction, a feature that


                                     12contrasts with the strong texture commonly observed in other PBF-LB processed alloys
[24,60] . At higher magniﬁcation, a reﬁned lath martensitic microstructure is evident,
containing a high density  of nanoscale carbides uniformly dispersed within the
martensitic matrix.

Etching with diﬀerent reagents reveals distinct aspects of the microstructure. Nital
preferentially attacks regions of varying carbon content and dislocation density, thereby
highlighting  the ﬁne  martensitic  substructure.  In  contrast,  picric  acid  etching
selectively reveals compositional variations associated with solidiﬁcation, making the
melt pool boundaries and primary dendritic features characteristic of the PBF-LB
process more apparent, see Figure 7.

Regarding the solidiﬁcation structure observed in PBF-LB, the morphology and size is
governed by the thermal gradient (G) and growth rate (R), with G/R determining the
morphology, and G * R determining the size. For the conditions experienced during
PBF-LB processing, iron-based alloys exhibit a ﬁne cellular or dendritic structure [61].

Tool steels typically exhibit a martensitic or bainitic structure but with a signiﬁcant
presence of retained austenite in the cellular boundaries and interdendritic regions [62].
This is due to the increased alloying content in the alloys and coupled with the micro-
segregation of elements during PBF-LB, leading to the chemical stabilization of the
austenite [63]. In terms of the martensitic matrix, the observed blocks are ﬁner due to
the typically higher carbon content present in these alloys [64]. Figure 8 shows the
typical microstructure of tool steels obtained from PBF-LB processing. Due to the
presence of RA, these materials typically undergo a heat treatment process in order to
decompose the austenite into ferrite [51].

3.4 Mechanical Properties

Owing to their reﬁned microstructure, PBF-LB processed low-alloy steels exhibit an
excellent balance of strength, ductility, and toughness. Several studies have reported
that  their mechanical  properties  are comparable  to,  or even  surpass,  those  of
conventionally processed counterparts [8,65,66], demonstrating the strong potential of
PBF-LB  fabricated  low-alloy  steels  for  applications  requiring  high  mechanical
performance.

From existing literature, several key observations have been made regarding directional
anisotropy in PBF-LB processed low alloy steels, with specimens exhibiting limited
directional anisotropy [6,8]. Mechanical anisotropy is a well-documented phenomenon
in PBF-LB processed Fe-based alloys and is primarily attributed to the formation of
large columnar grains oriented perpendicular to the loading direction in vertically built
specimens [60]. However, in low-alloy steels, the extent of anisotropy is considerably
reduced due to the martensitic transformation, which reﬁnes the microstructure and
disrupts the preferred crystallographic orientation developed during solidiﬁcation [7].
However, in a case where there is a presence of preferentially oriented defects, often
oriented perpendicular to the build direction, anisotropy can be observed. Studies have
also shown that  this behavior can be mitigated, at  least  partially, through the
application of suitable post-processing heat treatments [31].

For PBF-LB processed tool steels, in addition to the reﬁned martensitic structure, ﬁne
dispersions of carbides provide secondary hardening and resistance to softening during
tempering, allowing these materials to maintain high strength and hardness even after

                                     14prolonged thermal exposure [64]. The high alloy content also enhances hardenability
and tempering resistance but reduces the toughness of the material [19]. The prolonged
high temperature strength is due to secondary carbide precipitation in combination
with the high dislocation densities observed in martensite [67]. Studies have shown that
the decomposition of RA during direct tempering causes a precipitation of carbides in
the melt pool and interdendritic boundaries, promoting secondary crack growth and
resulted in higher fracture toughness [68]. Thermal fatigue resistance is another factor
to consider for tool steels due to their repeated thermal cycling experienced during
application. In  this regard,  it was again shown that  directly tempered material
exhibited better resistance against the formation of thermal fatigue cracks (heat
checks) [69].

In summary, hardness, wear resistance, and thermal stability are of importance for tool
steels, while toughness, ductility, and strength are emphasized for low-alloy steels. The
choice between the two depends on whether performance under high temperature and
wear conditions (typical for tooling applications), or a good combination

and toughness (typical for structural applications) is required for the application.

3.5 Challenges in PBF-LB Processing

PBF-LB processing of both low alloy and tool steels remains challenging due to their
poor printablility, primarily governed by the carbon content and the resulting residual
stress accumulation during fabrication [70]. The extreme thermal gradients and rapid
solidiﬁcation generate substantial internal stresses as newly deposited layers rapidly
cool and contract while being constrained by the underlying solidiﬁed material [25]. In
steels with elevated carbon content, these  stresses are further ampliﬁed by the
formation of brittle untempered martensite upon cooling. The high carbon fraction
increases hardenability and strength but also raises the material’s susceptibility to cold
cracking,  distortion, and  delamination,  especially  in  the  absence  of  build-plate
preheating [71]. Furthermore, residual stresses not only drive crack initiation but also
promote warping and dimensional inaccuracy, limiting the achievable build height and
component geometry.

Studies  have  shown  that  reducing  the  carbon  content  signiﬁcantly  improves
processability by lowering the transformational stresses generated during rapid cooling
[69]. When combined with optimized processing parameters and the application of
build-plate preheating, this approach enables the fabrication of fully dense, crack-free
components with high structural integrity and dimensional stability [69]. For tool
steels, alloy design strategies have been developed to enhance processability under the
rapid solidiﬁcation conditions of PBF-LB. One such approach involves increasing the

                                     15alloying  content  to  stabilize  austenite and  reduce  the  martensite  start  (Mₛ)
temperature, thereby counteracting the stresses generated during cooling. These alloys,
referred to as  “low transition temperature” tool  steels, undergo a more gradual
martensitic transformation, reducing the likelihood of cracking and distortion [72].

Another challenge is the cost associated with PBF-LB processing, whereby they diﬀer
for low-alloy and tool steels. For low-alloy steels, feedstocks are typically cheaper due
to the lower alloying content in comparison to tool steels, with the costs mainly
determined by machine time. To justify the use of PBF-LB for low-alloy steels, higher
throughput is essential. Increasing layer thickness or scan speed boosts productivity
but can reduce density and degrade mechanical properties; consequently, process
parameters must be optimized to balance quality and cost.

Tool  steels on the other hand rely on alloy design for AM, strategies for crack
mitigation, and optimized heat-treatment workﬂows; moreover, because tool steels are
ultimately qualiﬁed for their performance i.e. hardness, wear resistance, hot strength,
and dimensional stability. To achieve this the dominant cost driver typically becomes
the post-processing heat treatments (austenitization, double/triple tempering and, in
some cases, cryogenic steps [72,73]) and typically outweighs any savings resulting from
build-time optimization.

4.2 PBF-LB Processing

For the low-alloy engineering  steel studied  in Paper  I, PBF-LB processing was
conducted using an EOS M290 machine (EOS GmbH). The machine was equipped
with a Yb-ﬁber laser, with a maximum powder of 400 W and was operated in a
continuous wave mode. The spot size of the laser was about 100 µm in diameter, with
a Gaussian energy distribution. A stripe scan strategy was employed, with a stripe

                                     17width of 5 mm, and a stripe overlap of 0.12 mm, with a scan rotation of 67 ° applied
in between the diﬀerent layers. The build plate pre-heating was varied between 25 °C
and 80 °C. Laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing and layer thickness were varied to
study process optimization in Paper I.

For the lean tool steel studied in Paper II, PBF-LB was conducted in a Renishaw AM
400, with optimized process parameters that were developed in an earlier study [69].
The applied parameters yielded samples which had a relative density of > 99.8%, when
measured using optical image analysis.

4.3 Sample Preparation and Metallography
PBF-LB processed specimens (10 x 10 x 10 mm3) were sectioned to reveal a plane
perpendicular to the top layer of the scan tracks. This surface was used for both defect
analysis and microstructural characterization. Prior to the analysis, the samples were
mounted in a conductive resin, in order to ease sample handling and further processing
to achieve optical quality surfaces. All grinding and polishing steps were done on a
Struers TegraPol polisher. The samples were ﬁrst ground using 500#, 1000#, 2000#
and 4000# SiC-papers (Struers), with a force starting at 25N, and reduced to 15 N for
the ﬁnal grinding steps. The steps were carried out for about 1 – 3 min, and were
sometimes repeated, based on the sample surfaces obtained after the preceding step.
The polishing steps were conducted using diamond suspensions carrying particles of
sizes 3 µm and 1 µm. The 3 µm polishing step was carried out on a MD-Mol cloth from
Struers, with the 1 µm polishing step performed on a MD-Nap cloth. These samples
were then used for quantiﬁcation of porosity using optical image analysis techniques
(detailed in Section 4.4). Further polishing was done on the samples using a colloidal
silica suspension  (0.05 µm),  prior to etching and  further  characterization using
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM). The oxide polishing step ensured a clean surface
prior to etching. Etching was performed primarily using 2% Nital (98 ml C2H5OH + 2
ml HNO3). This etchant reveals the martensitic structure formed as a result of the
PBF-LB processing. Additionally, 1.3% Picric acid (1.3 g C6H3N3O7 in 100 ml H2O +
0.6 g C12H25NaO4S), modiﬁed with a surfactant (sodium lauryl sulphate, C12H25NaO4S)
to ensure wettability, was used to reveal a dendritic structure. Samples were typically
rinsed with ethanol and dried using a heat gun prior to microscopy.

electrolytic method. Manually thinned down foils (thickness of ~ 300 µm) were cut into

1. Introduction
Maraging steels are a class of high-performance iron-based (Fe) alloys used extensively in
applications requiring high strength-to-weight ratios, thin structural cross-sections, or high
toughness [1–5]. Example uses include rocket motor casings, load cells, torsion-bar suspensions,
aircraft landing gear, manufacturing tooling (dies and molds), and bearings. Most applications
stem from the combination of strength and toughness maraging steels exhibit [2,4,5].


These desirable properties originate from the two-step processing route of these alloys.
Maraging steels are first solutionized and quenched to form a martensitic matrix [6,7]. This “soft”
martensite is subsequently hardened via precipitation heat treatment to create dispersed, fine
precipitate phases and establish short and/or long-range atomic ordering [8,9]. This two-step
process of “martensite aging” creates microstructures with high strength, high ductility (relative
to the strength of the alloy), and thereby high toughness. Achieving these performance
characteristics require a series of specific alloying elements. High nickel (Ni) contents, often
greater than 10 wt. % to 15 wt. %, are required to readily form a martensitic matrix in traditional
processing routes. For example, the widely used C300 maraging steel (also identified as M300)
uses 18 wt. % Ni. Ni is also a core component in several precipitates in maraging steels, commonly
with a Ni3X stoichiometry [10,11].

Traditional maraging steels also require ~ 10 wt. % cobalt (Co) and ~ 5 wt. % molybdenum (Mo)
to achieve maximum precipitation strengthening. Co and Mo exhibit a synergistic effect with each
other,  drastically increasing the  precipitation strengthening of Mo-based  precipitates  in
martensite [12,13]. Individually adding Co or Mo does not produce nearly the same strengthening
effect. Ti and Al are often added as supplemental precipitate forming elements, but in quantities
far smaller than Ni, Co, or Mo. Ti is known to have a weaker, secondary effect in improving Mo
precipitation, but still establish considerable strengthening comparable to Co-additions. Because
of this, Ti is the primary precipitate element in the Co-free T-series maraging steels [13].

This combination of core alloying elements creates challenges for using maraging steels. Co and
Mo are costly, with market prices ranging from $24,300 to $82,000 and $44,300 to $83,770 per
metric ton, respectively, over the last 2 years at the time of writing in late 2024 (according to the
London Metal Exchange). These two elements are the most expensive alloying additions in
maraging steels, dwarfing the cost of $15,800 to $43,000 per metric ton for Ni. Such prices
economically restrict maraging steels to only the most-critical applications and prevent many
industries from cost-effectively utilizing the engineering potential of these alloys. Reliably
sourcing Co is also problematic. Nearly 75% of the Co mined in 2023 originated from the
Democratic Republic of Congo, making Co effectively sourced from a single country [14].
Geopolitical and supply chain risks mean the loss of Co from Congo would prevent critical
industries from functioning across the globe. This is further compounded by the increased use of
Cobalt in electric vehicles and energy storage applications, putting additional strain on this fragile
supply chain.

                                              1NIST IR 8582
July 2025


In recognition of these risks, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) has designated Co as a
critical mineral to incentivize contingencies for economic resilience in the case of restricted Co
access [15]. In response to growing concerns about occupational exposure to hazardous
substances, the European Union adopted Directive (EU) 2022/431, which amends Directive
2004/37/EC on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens or
mutagens at work. Among its provisions, the Directive mandates that the European Commission
propose, where appropriate, occupational exposure limits for cobalt and inorganic cobalt
compounds. These proposed limits are to be grounded in the latest scientific evidence and
developed in consultation with relevant stakeholders [16].


These challenges are not exclusive to the present day. Prior work in the 1980’s evaluated the
metallurgical impact of removing Co from maraging steels in response to supply chain shocks.
Sha et  al. analyzed the commercial Co-free, Ti-precipitation strengthened alloy T300 and
observed a considerable reduction in Fe-Mo based precipitation [10]. Hickey et al. found this
change had negligible impacts on the mechanical properties of T300 when compared to C300
series alloys [12,17]. This finding was attributed to Ti creating sufficient Ni3Ti and Fe-Mo
precipitates to generate equivalent strengthening. However, the Co-free alloys had reduced
corrosion  resistance with respect to the  Co-containing  alloys,  potentially  limiting  their
applications. T-series maraging steels have lagged C-series alloys in application for unclear
reasons, meaning the economic resiliency provided by their metallurgical constituency has not
been realized yet.


Additionally, recent supply chain disruptions combined with the European Chemicals Agency’s
(ECHA) classification of cobalt (Co) as a carcinogenic substance have intensified regulatory
pressure to eliminate cobalt from alloy formulations [18]. This has, in turn, driven the
development of a second generation of cobalt-free maraging steels, which differ from alloys like
T300 in that they contain appreciable amounts of chromium (Cr), making them more corrosion
resistant than existing maraging steels [19,20]. Example alloys in this space include M789 and
Mar-50. However, Cr additions restrict the formation of the Fe-Mo precipitates seen in C300 and
T300 alloys, forming instead G-phase precipitates (Ni16Ti6Si7) [21–24]. The G-phase provides less
strengthening compared to Fe-Mo precipitates, leading to reduced strengths but increased
ductility for the second generation of Co-free maraging steels.


Existing engineering designs using maraging steels expect the high strength of Co-containing
maraging steels. Thus, the strength debit from adding Cr prevents the immediate adoption of
new Co-free maraging steels despite the cost and safety benefits. New metallurgical processing
routes are needed to increase the strength of Co-free, Cr-containing maraging steels. Additive
manufacturing (AM) is one such route. The rapid solidification, non-equilibrium partitioning,
unique phase transformations, and thermal cycling of AM builds are new processing avenues to
create novel microstructures able to boost the performance of Co-free, Cr-containing maraging

steels. Many second-generation Co-free maraging steels were made to create custom tooling via
metal AM, implying that a robust commercial supply already exists for these materials.


This study lays the groundwork towards reaching performance parity between both Co-free, Cr-
containing alloys, and their Co-containing, Cr-free counterparts. Here, AM builds of the new Co-
free maraging  steel, M789, are manufactured to identify the most desirable processing
parameters towards this goal. Changes in solidification conditions and solid-state microstructure,
were experimentally measured. Mechanical properties of as-built material for each tested
parameter set were also measured. This research focuses on identifying the unique attributes of
each  as-built microstructure  that could  potentially provide a pathway to improve the
performance of Co-free, Cr-containing alloys, or prime the alloy for improved properties via post-
build heat treatments.

A melt pool forms as the laser scans over a pattern line for a fixed laser power and speed (Fig.

2). This melt pool has a width and depth which is affected predominantly by the laser power

and laser speed. For example, higher laser speed for a fixed power can lead to shallower and

narrower melt pools. Another important parameter is hatch spacing which is the distance

between two adjacent pattern lines. This is also ultimately the distance between two adjacent

melt pools. It is important to have sufficient overlap between the adjacent melt pools to avoid

the formation of a lack of fusion porosity. Finally, layer thickness is another parameter that

determines the amount of material that needs to be melted. A typical layer thickness is about

20 to 40 µm but higher layer thicknesses such as 80 to 120 µm are used for boosting

productivity. However, higher layer thickness also leads to lower feature resolution and higher

surface roughness. A combined parameter called volumetric energy density (VED) is used to

represent the main process parameters, see Eqn. (1).

    2.3.   Scan strategies in PBF-LB

Apart from the laser parameters mentioned above, scan strategy is another crucial parameter.

Scan strategy can be referred to as the pattern of the scan vectors that a laser follows in a layer.

Additionally, one can also rotate the scan vectors for the following layer. A plethora of scan

strategies can be employed for the PBF-LB process and some of the scan strategies are shown

in Fig. 3.

The choice of the scan strategy is crucial as it can lead to different microstructures and defect

distribution. Using a unidirectional scan strategy can lead to a highly textured microstructure

with columnar grains along the build direction. Employing a scan rotation of 90° (Fig. 3d) for

successive layers can aid in reducing the anisotropy, lowering residual stresses, and generating

a more fine-grained microstructure [6,7]. A stripe scan strategy (Fig. 3f) is commonly used

with a scan rotation of 67°. This leads to further reducing anisotropy and breaking down the

columnar microstructure [7].

The choice of scan strategy can be crucial for certain alloy systems that are more susceptible

to in-process cracking (hot cracking). Certain studies have shown that obtaining fine equiaxed

microstructure can reduce hot cracking in superalloys [8,9]. On the other hand, other studies

[10] have shown that having a lower fraction of high angle grain boundaries (HAGB) and a

higher fraction of low angle grain boundaries (LAGB) is beneficial in minimizing hot cracks

as they usually are found in HAGB.


                                     5In summary, scan strategy is a crucial parameter that could enable defect-free processing with

suitable microstructure for intended applications for certain alloys.





Figure 3. Schematic of selected scan strategies in PBF-LB (a) unidirectional scan strategy, (b)
bidirectional scan strategy, (c) chessboard scan strategy, (d) scan rotation of 90° for
bidirectional scan strategy, (e) scan rotation of 67° for bidirectional scan strategy (f) stripe
scan strategy

    2.4.   Microstructure evolution in PBF-LB

The rapid melting and solidification of the PBF-LB process leads to unique microstructures.

These microstructures are similar to welding rather than casting or forging. This is due to the

similar characteristics of PBF-LB and welding where there is a presence of a moving heat

source that melts and fuses material causing the presence of a fusion zone and a heat affected

zone. Hence, PBF-LB can be considered as a ‘multi-pass micro-welding’, and a part is

manufactured from thousands of melt pools. The temperature gradient and high cooling rate

within a melt pool affect the dislocation density, solidification structure, and grain morphology.

Furthermore, the elemental segregation is limited to the fine solidification structure. There are

possibilities of having different solidification morphologies and this is influenced by the

temperature gradient (G) and growth rate (R) as shown in Fig. 4 [11].

When the laser interacts with the metal powder a molten melt pool is formed which then

solidifies. The grains formed from the solidifying melt pool are influenced by the underlying

                                     6grains from the build plate or previously solidified material. This is called epitaxial grain

growth which leads to the formation of columnar grains which can span several layers. The

grains are also preferably oriented parallel to the build direction which is the reason for the

<100> crystallographic texture mostly observed in face centered cubic (FCC) materials

manufactured by PBF-LB.





Figure 4. Schematic showing the influence of temperature gradient and growth rate on the
solidification mechanism. Adapted from [11].

    2.5.   Defects in PBF-LB

Materials produced by PBF-LB can have certain types of defects. These defects are highly

influenced by the choice of process parameters for the PBF-LB process. Some of the commonly

observed defects in PBF-LB samples are lack of fusion, keyhole, and gas porosity [12] (shown

in Fig. 5). Lack of fusion porosity occurs when there is insufficient overlap between adjacent

melt pools in the same layer or between layers. This can be mitigated by having sufficient

overlap between the melt pools in a layer or between layers. Within a layer, this can be done

by reducing the hatch spacing to have sufficient overlaps or by fine-tuning the laser power and

speed to have a larger melt pool. Lack of fusion porosity is irregular in shape and has sharp

corners which can be detrimental for dynamic loading. Keyhole porosity may form due to the

material evaporation and recoil pressure at the bottom of the keyhole. This type of porosity is

spherical and can be reduced by increasing the laser speed or reducing the laser power to lower

the energy input [13]. Gas porosity is formed from entrapped gas from powder particles in melt

                                     7pools and is spherical. The gas porosity is typically smaller than the keyhole and is much more

random than the keyhole porosity. In addition to the defects mentioned above, microcracks can

also occur in certain alloys (Fig. 5c). This type of defect will be covered in detail in Section

3.2.

Superalloys are a class of materials developed for high temperature applications involving high

mechanical loads and are required to have high corrosion and oxidation resistance. These alloys

have excellent properties at high temperatures and are widely used in gas turbine applications.

In fact, the constant drive for gas turbine efficiency has been the driving force for the

development and innovations within this material class. Apart from gas turbines, superalloys

are also used in rocket engines, nuclear reactors, steam power plants, and petrochemical

equipment.  Superalloys  are  further  classified  into  Ni-base,  Co-base, and  Ni-Fe-base

superalloys. This classification is primarily based on the major base element (matrix) used in

the alloy [14].

Superalloys can broadly be divided into weldable and non-weldable alloys. This classification

is based on the amount of γ’ formers (Al and Ti) and is adapted from the weldability diagram

by Prager and Shira (Fig. 6a). Although it was developed for welding, it is still applicable to

Here the x-axis contains other γ’ formers such as Nb and Ta and this expression is proportional

to the predicted γ’ equilibrium volume fraction at 700 °C. The y-axis is the Scheil solidification

range which can serve as an indication for hot cracking risk.

    3.1.   Alloying elements

Superalloys have an FCC crystal structure (γ phase) with different alloying elements. These

elements could have multiple beneficial effects such as strengthening (solid solution or

precipitate), formation of beneficial phases, or improve certain high temperature properties.

For example, Cr is a crucial alloying element added for corrosion and oxidation resistance. Al,

Ti, Ta, and Nb are added to form the strengthening precipitate γ’ or γ’’ (in certain cases). Al is

also vital due to the formation of the protective oxide Al2O3. Certain elements such as Cr, Al,

Co, Mo, W, and Ta also contribute as solid solution strengtheners. C in conjunction with

elements such as Cr, Ti, Nb, Mo, Hf, and Ta form carbides (such as MC, M23C6, and M6C)

which also contribute to strengthening. Additions of Hf, B, and Zr have also been found to

contribute  to  grain boundary strengthening and improve high temperature mechanical

properties like creep and stress rupture [14].

    3.2.   Cracking mechanisms in Superalloys

High γ’ superalloys are susceptible to cracking either during welding or certain AM processes.

The cracking can be broadly divided into hot cracking and solid-state cracking. Hot cracking

includes solidification and liquation cracking. This type of cracking occurs during the welding

or AM processing. Solid-state cracking occurs during heat treatment of welded or AM

components. It is further divided into ductility dip cracking and strain age cracking. These

cracking mechanisms were identified and documented in welding and to some extent also apply

to the PBF–LB process. It is to be noted that hot cracking has also been observed in certain

solid-solution strengthened alloys such as Hastelloy X [25] and Haynes 230 [26].

    3.2.1.  Solidification cracking

Solidification is an important step in welding or AM process and solidification cracking can

occur within a solidifying melt pool. This type of cracking occurs during the last stages of

solidification within a melt pool when the liquid film is distributed along the grain boundaries

or in the inter-dendritic region. At such a stage the melt pool tends to contract due to the

solidification shrinkage and thermal contraction. The surrounding material also contracts but

not to the same extent as the melt pool. This leads to the formation of tensile stresses developed

across solidifying grains and/or inter-dendritic regions. If the stresses exceed the strength of


                                     10the  solidified  material, then  the  solidification crack  occurs. This type of cracking  is

characterized by a dendritic morphology surface [27,28].

    3.2.2.  Liquation cracking

Liquation cracking is a type of hot cracking that occurs due to the local melting of grain

boundary constituents in the partially melted zone (PMZ). Liquation cracking sometimes is

also referred to as HAZ (heat affected zone) liquation cracking as it occurs at the heat affected

zone of a melt pool. Liquation cracking can occur owing to two different mechanisms – the

segregation mechanism and the penetration mechanism. On one hand, the segregation

mechanism occurs due to the segregation of certain alloying elements (such as S, P and B) to

the grain boundaries. This reduces the local melting temperature which is affected by the heat

in the HAZ which may lead to the formation of a liquation crack due to the tensile stresses. On

the other hand penetration mechanism occurs when secondary phases (eutectic, intermetallics,

carbides, etc) do not have enough time for dissolution and can react with the matrix to form a

liquid film which under tensile stresses undergoes cracking [28].

    3.2.3.  Ductility Dip Cracking (DDC)

Ductility dip cracking (DDC) is a form of solid-state cracking reported to occur due to a loss

in ductility in superalloys. This loss is known to occur in a temperature range of half of the

solidus temperature up to the solidus temperature. The shrinkage strains occurring in and

around the weld can lead to the local exhaustion of ductility and lead to DDC [28].

    3.2.4.  Strain Age Cracking (SAC)

All the cracking mechanisms mentioned until now can occur in both solid-solution and

precipitation strengthened superalloys. But strain age cracking (SAC) exclusively occurs in

precipitation strengthened superalloy. SAC is a solid-state cracking and occurs during post-

processing heat treatment, although it is also possible to occur during reheating of multi-pass

welds. This cracking is prevalent in high γ’ (Ni3(Al, Ta, Ti)) precipitation strengthened Ni-base

superalloy and is proportional to the Al+Ti content in the alloy. These alloys must be solution

annealed before the aging step and it is almost impossible to avoid γ’ precipitation due to the

high Al+Ti content. So, residual stresses along with stresses caused due to the γ’ precipitation

lead to strain age cracking. This type of cracking is the main reason for classifying high γ’ Ni-

base superalloys as ‘non-weldable’.





                                     11    3.3.   Challenges in PBF-LB of Superalloys
    3.3.1.  Micro-cracking

Certain heritage superalloys with high γ’ volume fraction such as IN939 [16,29], IN738LC

[30–32] and CM247LC [16,29,33–36] are heavily alloyed and have reported micro-cracking

observed in samples produced using PBF-LB. This type of micro-cracking is hot cracking, in

particular, solidification cracking that occurs due to the increased solidification intervals. One

way of reducing/eliminating  solidification cracking  is  to have an  alloy with reduced

solidification interval. This means that certain elements have to be removed to reduce the

solidification interval and in turn mitigate solidification cracking. For example, some studies

have shown that reducing/eliminating elements such as B, Zr and Hf reduced the solidification

interval and thus the solidification cracking [32,36].  It is highly possible that the creep

properties could be affected as these elements are crucial for grain boundary strengthening

[37,38]. There have been attempts to design novel alloys that have eliminated solidification

cracking [16,24,39–42], but these alloys need rigorous testing before they can replace the

heritage alloys for industrial applications.

Another way is to optimize the process parameters to minimize solidification cracking. Studies

have demonstrated that narrower and shallower melt pools with short hatch spacing lead to less

or no cracking in PBF-LB [17,43]. This is not unique to the PBF-LB process but welding

literature has shown welds with low depth-to-width ratio to be beneficial [27]. This has been

attributed to the reduction in the solidification stresses and reduced segregation for welding.

This probably is valid for PBF-LB as well, however, the solidification structure and in turn

grain morphology also play a major role. Minimizing the high angle grain boundaries can

minimize the solidification cracking. This can be explained based on the model by Rappaz [44]

where high angle grain boundaries are more susceptible to liquid film presence at lower

temperatures. Hence, minimizing high angle grain boundaries can lead to lower solidification

cracking. Also, other techniques such as build plate pre-heating [45], modified scan strategy

[10] and adding grain refiners or nanoparticles [9,26,46] can aid in minimizing solidification

cracking. Furthermore, post-processing heat treatments such as hot isostatic pressing (HIP) can

heal solidification cracking [47,48].

    3.3.2.  Residual stresses

Residual stresses are stresses present in a material and are self-balanced without external

stresses. The localized energy input, constrained shrinkage, and the complex thermal history

induce residual stresses in parts built by the PBF-LB process. These residual stresses are high

                                     12and can cause deformation when certain parts are removed

## 1. vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 29-34 (Context ID: pqac-00000009)
