Appendix A. Scanning kelvin probe force microscopy (SKPFM)
Scanning kelvin probe force microscopy (SKPFM) measurements were completed to qualitatively
assess local corrosion differences in as-built material for parameter set A. SKPFM was performed
with a nominal 2.8 N/m cantilever with Pt/Ir coating for conductivity and a resonance frequency
of 75 kHz. SKPFM measurements were performed in double-pass, amplitude-modulation mode
with a typical lift height of 5 nm compared to the tapping mode first pass. The small lift height
ensured the tip was held close to the sample surface for enhanced spatial resolution and reduced
long range electrostatic forces acting on the cantilever body. SKPFM data was leveled by aligning
rows through a first order polynomial fitting.

SKPFM analysis and STEM imaging were both completed on build parameter set A to better
understand the as-built microstructure and identify any unique characteristics useful to
improving the performance of these alloys. Spatially correlated SKPFM was completed on a
microstructural region previously identified by SEM BSE imaging. The two high contrast features
(increased height in Figure 14B) are surface contamination whose shape and position are
readily identifiable in Figure 14. The use of these fiducials (the larger of which is indicated with
an arrow) show that the height maps generated from SKPFM contained cellular-like features
thought to be similar to those observed in Figure 4B, lending confidence to the presence of
retained γ-austenite cells throughout the microstructure.





   Figure 14: SKPFM map of the as-built microstructure from build parameter set A. A) BSE SEM image of the
    analyzed area with low Z-particles and fiduciary features present. B) Height map from the scanned area,
  showing cellular-like structures not visible in BSE imaging. C) Surface potential map showing minimal-to-no
                     change in expected corrosion behavior in the surveyed region.





                                             26NIST IR 8582
July 2025

Appendix B. X-ray computed tomography (XCT)

As-built porosity defects were characterized for Parameter sets A and C using X-ray computed
tomography (XCT) with 140 kV and 80 µA on a North Star Imaging X50 machine here with 6.60
µm/pixel ± 0.33 µm/pixel spatial resolution. All XCT data was post-processed using eFX1 Software
Suite Version 2.3.4 to quantify defect volume  fractions and  spatial  distribution. Defect
characterization was completed only for parameter sets A and C where defect density was
expected to be the lowest and highest, respectively. Data visualization was completed using
ParaView [44].

The shape of the external surfaces, as well as the internal pores, along the gauge sections of the
Specimens A and C were characterized using X-ray computed tomography (XCT). The XCT
measurements were performed using a North Star Imaging X50 machine. A resolution of 6.60
µm/pixel ± 0.33 µm/pixel was chosen, and the entire gauge section was imaged within a single
field-of-view (FOV). Specimens A and C were measured simultaneously (in the same FOV) to
reduce the acquisition time of the X-ray radiographs. X-ray transparent material (i.e., folded
paper) was sandwiched between the specimens to ensure that the individual specimens could be
easily  separated  and  identified  during  post-processing  of  the  reconstructed  images.
Reconstruction of the radiographs was also completed using North Star Imaging (proprietary)
software: efX Software Suite Version 2.3.4. Additional settings used during the acquisition of the
XCT radiographs can be found in Table A1.

The reconstructed images were further post-processed using IMPPY3D [45], which is an open-
source Python library developed at NIST. First, the ring artifacts were removed from the grayscale
images, followed by non-local means denoising [46]. Then, the images were segmented using a
global threshold value, resulting in a binarized image stack where white pixels correspond to
solid, metallic material. A before-and-after example of segmenting a reconstructed image is
illustrated in Figure 15 .

After segmentation, the image stack was converted into a three-dimensional (3D) voxel model.
Each voxel represents an extruded pixel implying an equal width, height, and length of 6.60 µm.
Fully enclosed pores were identified by inverting the values of the segmented image stack. Due
to the memory demand required to store so many voxels, the 3D models of Specimens A and C
were transformed into surface meshes using the marching cubes algorithm [47]. Individual pores
were left as voxels however. Quantitative metrics were also calculated from the segmented
images, such as equivalent spherical volumes of the pores and the overall porosity of the
specimens.


                              Table A1: Summary of nominal XCT parameters
             Accelerating voltage                           140 kV
            Accelerating amperage                           80 µA


                                             27NIST IR 8582
July 2025

         Radiograph exposure time                               2.5 s
              Voxel edge length                                6.60 µm
        Radiographs taken about 360°                        2400
       Num. radiographs averaged                           4
             Image bit depth                                     14-bit
           Thickness of copper filter                            1.27 mm





   Figure 15: Before a) and after b) images of X-ray computed tomography data processing of as-built defects.


As-built defects were characterized in the parameter sets with the hypothesized smallest and
largest defect volumes (A & C, respectively). Example as-built defects in parameter sets A (0.001
% porosity by volume) and C (0.071 % porosity by volume) are presented in Figure 16 of the
gauge region of mini-tensile specimens from XCT. The effect of increased scanning speed is
immediately clear between the two scans, with parameter set C having considerably larger and
more frequent defects than parameter set A. These findings highlight how the mechanical
performance of the as-built M789 will vary significantly between parameter sets A and C despite
the as-built microstructure remaining largely the same. Parameter sets B and D also exhibited
larger and more frequent defects than A or E, also likely leading to reduced mechanical
performance compared to the closer-to-ideal parameter sets. Given the small sampling volume,
only qualitative trends between parameter sets are discussed here.

These findings suggest that build parameter selection to minimize defects in AM builds can be
prioritized when using M789. The as-built microstructure is remarkably consistent despite the
large change in thermal history, potentially due to M789’s low martensite start temperature and


                                             28NIST IR 8582
July 2025

aspects of the  δ-ferrite to γ-austenite phase transformation. This finding means defect
minimization can be prioritized without risking the formation of detrimental microstructures,
enabling the easy manufacture of parts from this alloy across build processes and machine
variants. Further work is planned to validate this idea.





    Figure 16: XCT illustrations of defects in build parameter set A and build parameter set C. Note the build
                                   direction is parallel to the tensile direction.

{"answer": "## Thermo-Calc AM Module versus LPBF measurements in steels

**Yes, but the direct comparisons I could verify are qualitative rather than rigorous validations of 316L porosity or printability windows.** The clearest DOI-bearing steel example compares simulated and imaged melt-pool geometries in M789 maraging steel. I could not verify a study reporting numerical predicted-versus-measured cross-section errors, pore fractions, or printability-window accuracy for **316L using the Thermo-Calc AM Module itself**. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000021)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

The **strongest direct comparison** is Saville *et al.*, *Priming additively manufactured cobalt-free maraging steels for improved properties through changes to as-built microstructure*, NIST IR 8582 (2025), **DOI: 10.6028/nist.ir.8582**. They simulated single raster tracks for five M789 LPBF parameter sets with the AM Module and examined corresponding etched/BSE-visible melt-pool cross-sections. The observed variation was broadly consistent with simulated trends—particularly comparable pools for sets A and E—but pools for B–D were difficult to delineate. The authors explicitly call the simulated geometries **estimates for qualitative trends**, not quantitative predictions or an experimentally established fit. Absorptivity and its calibration are **not reported**. XCT separately measured **0.001 vol.% porosity for A and 0.071 vol.% for C**; the module did **not** predict those pore fractions. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000035)

A **closely related low-alloy-steel example** is Vaddamanu’s 2025 Chalmers licentiate work on SSAB AM Engineering martensitic steel. It explicitly uses Thermo-Calc 2025a’s AM Module with *calibrated heat sources* for 30- and 90-µm-layer single-track thermal simulations, while measuring top-layer melt-pool depth and image-based porosity. Experimentally, specimens achieved **at least 99.9% relative density across 75–180 J mm⁻³**. The examined thesis reports **neither a numerical calibrated absorptivity nor a predicted-versus-measured melt-pool error or module-predicted density window**: the measured processing window should not be presented as a validated AM Module prediction. answer.answer:
Yes. ## Thermo-Calc AM Module versus LPBF measurements in steels

**Yes, but the direct comparisons I could verify are qualitative rather than rigorous validations of 316L porosity or printability windows.** The clearest DOI-bearing steel example compares simulated and imaged melt-pool geometries in M789 maraging steel. I could not verify a study reporting numerical predicted-versus-measured cross-section errors, pore fractions, or printability-window accuracy for **316L using the Thermo-Calc AM Module itself**. (saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 12-17, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 17-23, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 1-2)

| Study / material / DOI | Thermo-Calc AM Module actually used? | Observables and comparison | Calibrated absorptivity | Agreement / limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Saville et al. (2025), M789 Co-free maraging steel**, NIST IR 8582; **DOI: [10.6028/NIST.IR.8582](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8582)** | **Yes.** TCFE10 + MOBFE5 properties were imported into the AM Module for steady-state single-raster-track simulations. | **Modeled:** relative melt-pool geometry and liquid–solid volume for five parameter sets (Fig. 3). **Measured:** BSE-visible melt-pool cross-sections (Fig. 6) and XCT porosity—**0.001 vol.%** for set A versus **0.071 vol.%** for set C. Porosity was measured, not predicted by the module. (saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 9-12, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 12-17, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured media cb59a453, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 30-34) | **Not reported; no experimental absorptivity calibration described.** | Qualitative trend agreement only: A and E had comparable observed and predicted pool sizes; B–D were less distinct, although parent-grain orientations were consistent with predicted trends. Authors explicitly call geometries “estimates” and say simulations were not intended for quantitative validation; no dimensional errors or porosity-prediction accuracy were reported. (saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 12-17, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 17-23) |
| **Vaddamanu (2025), SSAB AM Engineering low-alloy martensitic steel**, Chalmers licentiate thesis; **no confirmed DOI**. Appended Paper I was still a manuscript; related conference paper DOI: [10.59499/EP246281555](https://doi.org/10.59499/EP246281555). | **Yes.** Thermo-Calc 2025a AM Module with TCFE14; transient single-track calculations used steady-state calibrated heat sources for 30 and 90 µm layers. (vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 29-34, vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 1-7) | **Measured:** top-layer melt-pool depth and optical-image porosity/relative density. Experiments found **≥99.9% relative density over 75–180 J mm⁻³**, with lack of fusion at low energy and no observed keyhole porosity or cold cracking in the stable window. **Modeled:** temperatures and heat-affected-zone histories; the text does not establish that the measured density window was predicted by the module. (vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 29-34, vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 34-39) | Heat source described as **calibrated**, but the **numerical absorptivity is not published** in the thesis text examined. | Closest steel example linking module calculations with measured melt-pool depths and densification, but no tabulated predicted-versus-measured dimensions, error metric, or module-derived printability-window validation is reported. Thus it is not a quantitative validation of cross-section, porosity, or window prediction. (vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 29-34, vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 34-39) |
| **Sheikh et al. (2024), 316 stainless steel and other alloys**, *npj Computational Materials*; **DOI: [10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x)** | **No.** Thermo-Calc supplied CALPHAD thermophysical properties; melt-pool dimensions came from the independent **Eagar–Tsai** model with **Gladush–Smurov** keyhole-depth correction. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 14-15, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 1-2) | Predicted lack-of-fusion, balling, keyhole and defect-free regions were benchmarked against published 316-steel printability observations. This is a useful 316 comparator, but not an AM Module validation. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 1-2, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 2-3) | Absorptivity was **estimated from Drude theory**, not calibrated as an AM Module parameter; the cited excerpt gives no alloy-specific numerical value. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 14-15) | Relevant to 316 printability maps, but must not be cited as evidence that Thermo-Calc’s commercial AM Module reproduced measured 316L melt-pool sections or porosity. The analytical models also omit fluid flow and temperature-dependent properties. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 14-15) |


*Table: Direct AM Module evidence is limited to qualitative or incompletely quantified steel comparisons; the best 316 printability example instead uses Thermo-Calc properties with separate analytical models. The reported 70% calibrated absorptivity belongs to CM247LC nickel superalloy—not steel—and is therefore excluded from the steel rows.*

It is therefore relevant corroboration for *Thermo-Calc-informed* printability modeling, **not** evidence of a validated 316L AM Module window. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 14-15, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 1-2, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 2-3)

contexts.context: This excerpt provides a potentially related paper: Mariam Assi et al., “Design and assessment of an austenitic stainless alloy for laser powder bed additive manufacturing,” Applied Sciences (2024), DOI 10.3390/app14198649. The study uses Thermo-Calc for Scheil solidification and equilibrium phase predictions, including a predicted single-FCC stability range of 950–1230 °C, but it does not identify use of the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module. It experimentally evaluates an optimized alloy manufactured by LPBF and compares some results with 316L. Reported measurements include LPBF porosity of 0.05% (standard deviation 0.02%), with pore sizes averaging 4.5 μm and not exceeding 10 μm; typical 316L porosity is cited as approximately 0.8–1%. The excerpt also reports measured thermal expansion for cast and LPBF versions of the optimized alloy and 316L. However, it contains no direct experimental comparison of Thermo-Calc AM Module predictions against measured melt-pool dimensions or cross sections, no calibrated laser absorptivity, and no goodness-of-fit analysis. Thus, it is relevant as a Thermo-Calc-assisted LPBF steel study with porosity data, but it does not directly satisfy the requested AM-Module validation criteria.

snippets: Our framework uses Thermo-Calc to derive CALPHAD-based thermophysical properties using the Property, Equilibrium and Scheil models.

For the case studies presented, the Thermo-Calc calculations are simplified where only two Thermo-Calc models and a single database are used: Property and Equilibrium Models with the TCHEA5 thermodynamic database.
Using the material properties derived from CALPHAD and ROM models, melt pool dimensions for alloys processed using L-PBF were calculated using the Eagar–Tsai model (E-T).
The material inputs for the E- T analytical model are thermal conductivity [W/m K], density [kg/m3], specific heat [J/kg K], melting (liquidus) temperature [K], and laser absorptivity.
We benchmark different sets of criteria for the onset of fabrication defects (total of 12) and compare the resulting maps with an exhaustive validation dataset.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an automated framework that obtains alloy thermophysical and related properties from CALPHAD/Thermo-Calc and supplements them with rule-of-mixtures (ROM) calculations. It explicitly states that properties are queried from Thermo-Calc and ROM, including thermal conductivity, density, effective specific heat, melting/liquidus temperature, boiling temperature, molecular weight, and related quantities. The melt-pool geometry is then calculated using analytical heat-transfer models: the Eagar–Tsai (E-T) model for length, width, and baseline depth, with the Gladush–Smurov (G-S) model used to correct melt-pool depth in keyhole conditions. The excerpt does not identify use of a commercial Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module specifically; it refers instead to CALPHAD-based properties, Thermo-Calc queries, ROM, and analytical E-T/G-S models. Absorptivity is estimated through Drude’s theory: η = 0.365√(ρ0/λ), where ρ0 is electrical resistivity and λ is laser wavelength; resistivity is queried at room temperature. No numerical absorptivity values, laser wavelengths, resistivities, or detailed experimental melt-pool measurements are provided in this excerpt. The text also notes that E-T and G-S omit fluid-flow effects and temperature-dependent properties, indicating modeling limitations rather than direct experimental determination.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone compared predictions of the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module with measured melt-pool cross-sections, porosity or printability windows for 316L stainless steel (or other steels) made by laser powder bed fusion? Give the closest examples with DOIs, the observables compared, the calibrated absorptivity, and how well the module agreed.

Yes. ## Thermo-Calc AM Module versus LPBF measurements in steels

**Yes, but the direct comparisons I could verify are qualitative rather than rigorous validations of 316L porosity or printability windows.** The clearest DOI-bearing steel example compares simulated and imaged melt-pool geometries in M789 maraging steel. I could not verify a study reporting numerical predicted-versus-measured cross-section errors, pore fractions, or printability-window accuracy for **316L using the Thermo-Calc AM Module itself**. (saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 12-17, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 17-23, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 1-2)

| Study / material / DOI | Thermo-Calc AM Module actually used? | Observables and comparison | Calibrated absorptivity | Agreement / limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Saville et al. (2025), M789 Co-free maraging steel**, NIST IR 8582; **DOI: [10.6028/NIST.IR.8582](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8582)** | **Yes.** TCFE10 + MOBFE5 properties were imported into the AM Module for steady-state single-raster-track simulations. | **Modeled:** relative melt-pool geometry and liquid–solid volume for five parameter sets (Fig. 3). **Measured:** BSE-visible melt-pool cross-sections (Fig. 6) and XCT porosity—**0.001 vol.%** for set A versus **0.071 vol.%** for set C. Porosity was measured, not predicted by the module. (saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 9-12, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 12-17, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured media cb59a453, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 30-34) | **Not reported; no experimental absorptivity calibration described.** | Qualitative trend agreement only: A and E had comparable observed and predicted pool sizes; B–D were less distinct, although parent-grain orientations were consistent with predicted trends. Authors explicitly call geometries “estimates” and say simulations were not intended for quantitative validation; no dimensional errors or porosity-prediction accuracy were reported. (saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 12-17, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 17-23) |
| **Vaddamanu (2025), SSAB AM Engineering low-alloy martensitic steel**, Chalmers licentiate thesis; **no confirmed DOI**. Appended Paper I was still a manuscript; related conference paper DOI: [10.59499/EP246281555](https://doi.org/10.59499/EP246281555). | **Yes.** Thermo-Calc 2025a AM Module with TCFE14; transient single-track calculations used steady-state calibrated heat sources for 30 and 90 µm layers. (vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 29-34, vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 1-7) | **Measured:** top-layer melt-pool depth and optical-image porosity/relative density. Experiments found **≥99.9% relative density over 75–180 J mm⁻³**, with lack of fusion at low energy and no observed keyhole porosity or cold cracking in the stable window. **Modeled:** temperatures and heat-affected-zone histories; the text does not establish that the measured density window was predicted by the module. (vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 29-34, vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 34-39) | Heat source described as **calibrated**, but the **numerical absorptivity is not published** in the thesis text examined. | Closest steel example linking module calculations with measured melt-pool depths and densification, but no tabulated predicted-versus-measured dimensions, error metric, or module-derived printability-window validation is reported. Thus it is not a quantitative validation of cross-section, porosity, or window prediction. (vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 29-34, vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 34-39) |
| **Sheikh et al. (2024), 316 stainless steel and other alloys**, *npj Computational Materials*; **DOI: [10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x)** | **No.** Thermo-Calc supplied CALPHAD thermophysical properties; melt-pool dimensions came from the independent **Eagar–Tsai** model with **Gladush–Smurov** keyhole-depth correction. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 14-15, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 1-2) | Predicted lack-of-fusion, balling, keyhole and defect-free regions were benchmarked against published 316-steel printability observations. This is a useful 316 comparator, but not an AM Module validation. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 1-2, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 2-3) | Absorptivity was **estimated from Drude theory**, not calibrated as an AM Module parameter; the cited excerpt gives no alloy-specific numerical value. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 14-15) | Relevant to 316 printability maps, but must not be cited as evidence that Thermo-Calc’s commercial AM Module reproduced measured 316L melt-pool sections or porosity. The analytical models also omit fluid flow and temperature-dependent properties. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 14-15) |


*Table: Direct AM Module evidence is limited to qualitative or incompletely quantified steel comparisons; the best 316 printability example instead uses Thermo-Calc properties with separate analytical models. The reported 70% calibrated absorptivity belongs to CM247LC nickel superalloy—not steel—and is therefore excluded from the steel rows.*

The **strongest direct comparison** is Saville *et al.*, *Priming additively manufactured cobalt-free maraging steels for improved properties through changes to as-built microstructure*, NIST IR 8582 (2025), **DOI: 10.6028/nist.ir.8582**. They simulated single raster tracks for five M789 LPBF parameter sets with the AM Module and examined corresponding etched/BSE-visible melt-pool cross-sections. The observed variation was broadly consistent with simulated trends—particularly comparable pools for sets A and E—but pools for B–D were difficult to delineate. The authors explicitly call the simulated geometries **estimates for qualitative trends**, not quantitative predictions or an experimentally established fit. Absorptivity and its calibration are **not reported**. XCT separately measured **0.001 vol.% porosity for A and 0.071 vol.% for C**; the module did **not** predict those pore fractions. (saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 9-12, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 12-17, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 17-23, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured media 4b960552, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured media cb59a453, saville2025primingadditivelymanufactured pages 30-34)

A **closely related low-alloy-steel example** is Vaddamanu’s 2025 Chalmers licentiate work on SSAB AM Engineering martensitic steel. It explicitly uses Thermo-Calc 2025a’s AM Module with *calibrated heat sources* for 30- and 90-µm-layer single-track thermal simulations, while measuring top-layer melt-pool depth and image-based porosity. Experimentally, specimens achieved **at least 99.9% relative density across 75–180 J mm⁻³**. The examined thesis reports **neither a numerical calibrated absorptivity nor a predicted-versus-measured melt-pool error or module-predicted density window**: the measured processing window should not be presented as a validated AM Module prediction. The relevant appended study was identified as a **manuscript**, with no DOI verified for that study. (vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 29-34, vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 34-39, vaddamanu2025powderbedfusionlaser pages 1-7)

**Important distinction for 316 steel:** Sheikh *et al.*, *npj Computational Materials* (2024), **DOI: 10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x**, benchmarks calculated printability maps against published observations that include 316 stainless steel. It obtains material properties from Thermo-Calc but calculates melt pools with **separate Eagar–Tsai and Gladush–Smurov analytical models**, **not** the commercial Thermo-Calc AM Module. Its absorptivity is estimated using Drude theory, not a measured module-calibration value. It is therefore relevant corroboration for *Thermo-Calc-informed* printability modeling, **not** evidence of a validated 316L AM Module window. (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 14-15, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 1-2, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 2-3)

Finally, a **70% calibrated absorptivity** does appear in a Thermo-Calc AM Module LPBF study, but its material is **CM247LC, a nickel-base superalloy**, not 316L or another steel; transferring that value to steel would be unjustified. (hussain2024powderbedfusion–laser pages 25-33)

info.query: Has anyone compared predictions of the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module with measured melt-pool cross-sections, porosity or printability windows for 316L stainless steel (or other steels) made by laser powder bed fusion?
